segments.translit: jñānānandasundaro hi lūipādas tam evārthaṃ viśeṣayati —
segments.translation: [Lūyī]{p-luyi}pāda, beautiful with the [joy]{ananda} of [knowledge]{jnana}, sets out that same meaning in its particulars:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as Lūyīpāda, beautiful with the joy of knowledge, setting out ‘that same meaning’ in its particulars (cp.29.m1). He does not say here which meaning he has in view. The Tibetan makes it ‘the meaning of reality’ (de kho na nyid kyi don), which it calls especially exalted.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi don khyad par du 'phags pa'i phyir gsungs te, ‘spoke because the meaning of reality is especially exalted’: it renders Munidatta's tam evārthaṃ, ‘that same meaning’, as ‘the meaning of reality’ (perhaps reading tattvārthaṃ, or expanding de kho na, ‘that very’, to de kho na nyid, ‘reality’) and takes viśeṣayati as ‘excel’ rather than ‘specify’ (cp.29.m1). I follow the Sanskrit.

viśeṣayati, ‘particularizes, specifies’ (cp.29.m1): rendered ‘sets out … in its particulars’; ‘distinguishes’ or ‘elaborates’ would also do. Munidatta does not say which earlier meaning ‘that same meaning’ refers to.

segments.translit: bhāva ṇa hoi ityādi | bhāvas tāvat tattvaṃ na bhavati | yasmāt piṇḍagrahāṇubhede vicāreṇa bhāvasyopalambho na vidyate | kim abhāvaśrutir bhavati | abhāvo 'pi na bhavati asadrūpatvāt | īdṛk sambodhane ko 'pi sattvaḥ tattvaṃ pratītikaroti |
segments.translation: ‘[Being]{bhava-being} does not come to be’ and so on. [Being]{bhava-being}, to begin with, is not [reality]{tattva}, since in [piṇḍagrāha and anubheda]{pindagraha-anubheda} [examination]{vicara} finds no [apprehension]{upalambha} of being. Does the word ‘[nonbeing]{abhava}’ apply, then? Nonbeing is not reality either, since it has the form of the unreal. In such an [awakening]{bodhi}, what sentient being at all puts its trust in reality?
segments.note: Munidatta reads 1a as denying that being or nonbeing is reality: examined in piṇḍagrāha and anubheda, completion-stage meditations of dissolution, being is not apprehended, and nonbeing has the form of the unreal. He takes hoi as ‘is (reality)’, not ‘comes to be’. His sambodhana, ‘awakening’, renders 1b's saṃbohem̐; the Tibetan has ‘buddha’ (cp.29.m2).

flags.note: piṇḍagrahāṇubhede (cp.29.m2). I follow the glossary entry: the two completion-stage meditations piṇḍagrāha, ‘holding as a whole’, and anubheda, ‘successive dissolution’ (keep-source-first-gloss), because Munidatta uses the same pair in the same construction, with examination and apprehension, at cp.21.m4 (spelled piṇḍagrāhānubhede there). The spelling here (short graha, retroflex ṇ) reads naturally as piṇḍagraha-aṇu-bheda, ‘splitting what is grasped as a mass into atoms’, the atomist argument he runs on song 26 (cp.26.m2); that would give ‘since, when what is grasped as a mass is divided into atoms, examination finds no apprehension of being’. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ril por 'dzin pa'i dbye ba med pa la, ‘where there is no division of holding as a whole’, as if reading abheda: ril por 'dzin pa is the usual Tibetan for piṇḍagrāha, and it has nothing for atoms (rdul phra rab) or for anubheda (usually rjes su gzhig pa). So the Tibetan supports piṇḍagrāha but neither anubheda nor aṇu.

kim abhāvaśrutir bhavati, ‘does the word nonbeing apply, then?’ (cp.29.m2): the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ci ste dngos por thob par 'gyur, ‘how would it be obtained as a thing?’, attached to the sentence before, as if reading bhāva rather than abhāva and a word for attaining where the Sanskrit has śruti, ‘hearing, word’. I follow the Sanskrit.

Song 1b saṃbohem̐: Munidatta renders it sambodhana in the locative, īdṛk sambodhane, ‘in such an awakening’ (cp.29.m2). That fits the draft's ‘awakening’ (bodhi) and its ‘in’, though sambodhana can also mean ‘making known, address’, so his word does not wholly exclude ‘such an explanation’. He has no buddha. The Tibetan line ('di 'dra'i sangs rgyas) and comment ('di 'dra ba'i rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas, ‘such a perfect buddha’) read ‘buddha’, as if sambuddha. His pratītikaroti, ‘puts trust in’, supports the draft's ‘believe’ for patiāi (Tibetan yid ches par byed).

Song 1a: Munidatta takes na hoi as ‘is not reality’ (tattvaṃ na bhavati) and says nonbeing too ‘is not’ (abhāvo 'pi na bhavati), giving no verb for ṇa jāi (cp.29.m2); the Tibetan line likewise has ‘it is not being, nor is it nonbeing’ (dngos po ma yin dngos po med pa'ang ma yin pa'i). The draft's ‘does not come to be … does not go’ keeps the song's verbs; the divergence is noted, not harmonized.

ko 'pi sattvaḥ (cp.29.m2): taken as a question echoing the song's ko patiāi, ‘who would believe?’; ko 'pi can also be indefinite, giving ‘some rare being comes to trust reality in such an awakening’. The Tibetan (sems can gang gis kyang … yid ches par byed) does not settle it.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena bhāvasvarūpadaurlabhyaṃ pratipādayati —
lūi bhaṇai ityādi | lūyīpādaḥ siddhācāryyo hi vadati | ata eva durlakṣaṃ tattvaṃ bālayoginā lakṣayituṃ na pāryyate | yasmāt traidhātukaṃ kāyavākcitte vilasati krīḍati | tasya santānadīrghahrasvaparimaṇḍalādikaṃ | na ūhe na jānāmi | [44ka] kutra niyataṃ vasatīti |
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he shows how hard the [true nature]{svarupa} of [being]{bhava-being} is to reach. ‘[Lūyī]{p-luyi} says’ and so on: the [siddha]{siddha} master [Lūyī]{p-luyi}pāda says: ‘For that very reason [reality]{tattva}, [hard to discern]{durlaksa}, cannot be discerned by a [novice yogin]{balayogin}, since it is at [play]{lila}, at sport, in the [three worlds]{trailokya}, in [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}. Its [continuum]{santana}, long, short, round and so on, I do not make out, that is, I do not know it: where does it stay fixed?’
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as saying that reality is beyond a novice yogin's discerning, since it plays in the three worlds, body, speech and mind; Lūyī cannot make out its continuum, long, short or round, nor where it stays (cp.29.m3). His novice yogin stands where the song has baṭa; his ‘I do not make out’ renders uha.

equations.en: body, speech and mind (kāyavākcitta), in apposition

flags.note: Song 2a baṭa: Munidatta's paraphrase has ‘by a novice yogin’ (bālayoginā) where the song has baṭa (cp.29.m3). That suits the draft's vaṭu, ‘lad’, a beginner, and not bāṭa, ‘road’; the Tibetan line has rmongs pa, ‘fool’, and the Tibetan comment byis pa'i rnal 'byor pa, ‘novice yogin’. But in his sentence the novice is the one who cannot discern (an instrumental agent), not someone addressed: his wording suggests baṭa as the subject (‘the lad cannot make it out’) rather than the draft's vocative. This is a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss.

Song 2a biṇāṇā: what Munidatta calls hard to discern is ‘reality’ (tattva), and he has no word for consciousness (vijñāna) (cp.29.m3). The Tibetan line has ya mtshan, ‘wonder’, there, and its comment de nyid, ‘reality’. His wording neither supports nor rules out the draft's ‘consciousness’; he may simply be naming what it refers to.

Song 2b uha: Munidatta writes na ūhe, glossed na jānāmi, ‘I do not know’ (cp.29.m3). He thus derives uha from Sanskrit ūh-, ‘reason, make out’, as the draft's ūha, ‘reasoning’, does, but as a first-person verb with an object (the continuum's shape, and where it stays): ‘I do not make out’, not ‘reasoning does not reach it’. He gives nothing for lāge. The Tibetan line has dbyibs dang spyod lam med, ‘it has no shape or bearing’, where the Bengali has uha lāge ṇā, and the Tibetan comment says ‘not knowing the shape (dbyibs)’, so the Tibetan seems to take uha as ‘shape’; Munidatta's long, short and round are shapes, which may be what it echoes.

traidhātukaṃ kāyavākcitte vilasati (cp.29.m3): the nominative traidhātukaṃ sits loosely beside the locative; I take the two as apposition, ‘in the three worlds, in body, speech and mind’. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) makes it an equation: khams gsum ni lus ngag yid gsum, ‘the three worlds are body, speech and mind’.
siddha (keep-source-first-gloss), first in this unit at cp.29.m3: an accomplished tantric adept; Munidatta calls Lūyīpāda a siddhācārya, ‘siddha master’.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena uktārthaṃ spaṣṭayati —
jāhera ityādi | yasya tattvasya varṇacihnarūpaṃ nāvagamyate so 'pi kathaṃ nānākāvye vinaya āgamaśāstre vede vyākhyāyate ca |
tathā ca nāgārjjunapādāḥ |
na raktapītamāñjīṣṭho varṇas tenopalabhyata ityādi |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he makes plain the meaning already stated. ‘That whose’ and so on: that [reality]{tattva} whose [colour]{varna}, [sign]{cihna} and [form]{rupa} are not understood, how is it explained in the various poems, in the [Vinaya]{tx-vinaya}, in [scripture]{agama} and treatises, and in the [Veda]{tx-veda}? And so [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna}pāda: ‘No colour, red, yellow or madder, is perceived by it’, and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as making the refrain plainer: reality, whose colour, sign and form are not understood, cannot be explained in poetry, the Vinaya, scripture and treatises, or the Veda, where the song names only scripture and Veda. He backs this with Nāgārjuna's line that no colour, red, yellow or madder, is perceived (cp.29.m4).

citations.work: a verse Munidatta ascribes to Nāgārjunapāda; work not named or identified

flags.note: Song 3a bāna: Munidatta's varṇacihnarūpa (cp.29.m4) confirms the draft's reading of bāna as varṇa, ‘colour’; the Tibetan line has kha dog, ‘colour’.

The Tibetan comment (Toh 2293) has gang gi de nyid kyi mtshan ma'i gzugs rtogs pa med pa, ‘whose reality's form of sign is not understood’, leaving out colour, and splits Munidatta's āgamaśāstre into lung dang bstan bcos, ‘scripture and treatises’ (cp.29.m4). I follow that split and mark only ‘scripture’ as agama, though the glossary lists āgamaśāstre as a form of agama.

tena in the quoted line (cp.29.m4): taken as ‘by it’; it could be ‘by him’ or ‘therefore’. The Tibetan (de mi dmigs, ‘that is not apprehended’) makes ‘that’ the thing not apprehended. Without the rest of the verse the referent is unclear.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena tattvasvarūpam āha —
kāhere ityādi | kasya kim uktvā pṛthakjanāya mayā siddhāntaḥ pradātavyaḥ | yathodakacandra[ḥ] na satyaṃ na mṛṣā bhavati tadvad yogīndrasya bhāvagrāmapratibhāsaḥ sa kimartho vaktuṃ yujyate | arthaḥ tatra pratītiṃ karoti | avacanatvāt |
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of [reality]{tattva}. ‘To whom’ and so on: to whom, saying what, am I to give a [settled doctrine]{siddhanta}, to an [ordinary person]{prthagjana}? As the [moon in water]{udakacandra} is neither true nor false, so too is the [appearance]{abhasa} of the host of things to the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}: why would it be fitting to speak of it? The thing itself brings conviction there, since it is [inexpressible]{avacana}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as stating reality's true nature: what settled doctrine could Lūyī give an ordinary person, and in what words, when what appears to the lord of yogis is, like the moon in water, neither true nor false, and is inexpressible (cp.29.m5)? His settled doctrine, something given, stands where the song has piricchā.

flags.note: Song 4a piricchā: Munidatta's paraphrase, ‘to whom, saying what, am I to give (pradātavyaḥ) a settled doctrine (siddhānta)’ (cp.29.m5), keeps the song's dibi as ‘give’ and puts siddhānta, a settled conclusion, where the song has piricchā, as if he heard something like pariccheda, ‘determination, decision’ (my guess), rather than pṛcchā, ‘question’. On his reading the line is about giving an answer, not putting a question as in the draft. He also adds ‘to an ordinary person’. The Tibetan line agrees with the draft: bdag gis dri bar bya, ‘shall I ask’.

bhāvagrāmapratibhāsaḥ (cp.29.m5): the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug sgom pa'i grong khyer gyi gzugs brnyan, ‘the reflection of the town of meditation of the lord of yogis’: it reads bhāvanā (sgom pa) for bhāva, takes grāma literally as ‘town’ (grong khyer) where bhāvagrāma is the idiom ‘host of things’, and renders pratibhāsa as gzugs brnyan, ‘reflection’, which suits the moon in water. I follow Munidatta's Sanskrit.

arthaḥ tatra pratītiṃ karoti (cp.29.m5): I translate the printed text as a statement, ‘the thing itself (artha) brings conviction there, since it is inexpressible’, that is, conviction comes from the thing, not from words. The Tibetan has yang na de la ji ltar yid ches par byed de smrar med pa'i phyir ro, ‘or else, how does one come to trust it, since it is inexpressible?’, as if reading athavā for arthaḥ and a question; that reading may be the better one.

kasya kim uktvā (cp.29.m5): the Tibetan has gang gis ci zhig grol te, ‘by whom, having released what’, as if reading kiṃ muktvā (the written kimuktvā allows it), and bar gyi grub mtha' ci zhig, ‘what intermediate tenet’, with no counterpart for bar gyi in Munidatta's Sanskrit. For sa kimartho vaktuṃ yujyate it has de ji ltar sbyar te bshad par bya, ‘how is it to be put together and explained?’, close in sense.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena cittasvarūpam āha —
lūi bhaṇai ityādi | vadati lūyīpādaḥ mayā bhāvyabhāvakabhāvanā abhāvena kiṃ bhāvyaṃ | ata eva yaś caturtharūpaṃ gṛhītvā tiṣṭhāmi tasyāpi guruvacanavicāre tasyoddeśaṃ na ūhe | na paśyāmi |
tathā ca | cittaṃ niści[45]tya bodhena abhyāsaṃ kurute yadā |
tathā ca | tadā tadā cittaṃ na paśyāmi kva gataṃ kva sthitaṃ bhavet ||29||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of [mind]{citta}. ‘[Lūyī]{p-luyi} says’ and so on: [Lūyī]{p-luyi}pāda says: ‘With [object of meditation and meditator]{bhavya-bhavaka} and [meditation]{bhavana} absent, what am I to meditate on? For that very reason, as for the fourth form that I have taken up and stay with, of that too, when it is put to [examination]{vicara} by the [guru]{guru}'s word, I do not make out its whereabouts, that is, I do not see it.’ And so: ‘When one has ascertained the mind through understanding and takes up [practice]{abhyasa}’; and so: ‘just then I do not see the mind: where could it have gone, where could it stay?’
segments.note: Munidatta reads the last couplet as stating the mind's true nature: with object, meditator and meditation absent, Lūyī has nothing to meditate on, and even the ‘fourth form’ he has taken up, examined by the guru's word, cannot be located or seen. A verse he quotes agrees: the mind, ascertained and practised, is not seen anywhere (cp.29.m6).

citations.quoted: cittaṃ niścitya bodhena abhyāsaṃ kurute yadā | … tadā tadā cittaṃ na paśyāmi kva gataṃ kva sthitaṃ bhavet
citations.work: unnamed verse, introduced only by tathā ca; not identified

flags.note: Song 5b uha: Munidatta's tasyoddeśaṃ na ūhe | na paśyāmi, ‘I do not make out its whereabouts, that is, I do not see it’ (cp.29.m6), again takes uha as the verb ūh-, first person, with an object, and has ‘see’ where the song has dis. On his reading 5b would run roughly ‘of what I have taken up and stay with, I do not make out (its place); it is not seen’, rather than ‘no reasoning appears’. He also names what was taken up: ‘the fourth form’. The Tibetan line has no word for uha (gang zhig blangs 'dug de ni bdag gis ma mthong ngo, ‘what has been taken up and stays, I do not see’); the Tibetan comment says its shape (dbyibs) is not shown, as at 2b. His kiṃ bhāvyaṃ, ‘what am I to meditate on?’, supports the draft's 5a.

caturtharūpaṃ, ‘the fourth form’ (cp.29.m6): the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rkang pa bzhi pa bzung nas bdag gnas pa, ‘having taken up the fourth pada, I stay’, as if reading caturthapada, the word that opens this comment (Tibetan rkang pa bzhi pas). Munidatta does not say what the fourth form is, and I have not supplied it.

The quoted verse (cp.29.m6) is printed with tathā ca before each half, though the first half (yadā, ‘when’) needs the second (tadā, ‘then’); the Tibetan quotes it as one four-line verse introduced once (de bzhin du yang). The Tibetan has de tshe once for tadā tadā (rendered ‘just then’), and gang du song zhing gang nas 'gyur, ‘where it went and whence it comes’, for kva gataṃ kva sthitaṃ bhavet, ‘where gone, where staying’.

yaś caturtharūpaṃ gṛhītvā tiṣṭhāmi (cp.29.m6): the relative yaḥ is masculine nominative, ‘I who’, which would make the later tasya refer to the speaker; I take it with the song's jā, ‘what’, as the fourth form taken up. Likewise na paśyāmi may render the song's ṇa dis rather than gloss na ūhe.

proposals.definition: Old Bengali uha (song 29, 2b and 5b), taken in the draft as Sanskrit ūha, ‘reasoning, conjecture’. Munidatta writes na ūhe, ‘I do not make out’, glossed ‘I do not know’ (cp.29.m3) and set beside ‘I do not see’ (cp.29.m6): he too derives it from ūh-, but as a first-person verb. The Tibetan line of 2b has dbyibs, ‘shape’.
proposals.rationale: The word recurs in 2b and 5b and Munidatta glosses it both times (cp.29.m3, cp.29.m6), so an entry would link the two lines with his glosses and record that its sense is doubtful. If the reviewer would rather leave the word unlinked, let it go; the equations then fall back to no term.

questions: piṇḍagrahāṇubhede (cp.29.m2): I follow the glossary's two completion-stage meditations, piṇḍagrāha and anubheda, because Munidatta uses the pair the same way at cp.21.m4. The spelling here suits ‘division into atoms’, and the Tibetan reads ‘where there is no division of holding as a whole’. Keep the technical reading, or translate ‘when what is grasped as a mass is divided into atoms’?

arthaḥ tatra pratītiṃ karoti (cp.29.m5): I translate the printed text as a statement, ‘the thing itself brings conviction there, since it is inexpressible’. The Tibetan reads a question, ‘or else, how does one come to trust it?’, as if athavā for arthaḥ. Which do you prefer?

Song 4a piricchā: Munidatta puts ‘give a settled doctrine’ where the song has dibi piricchā (cp.29.m5), against the draft's ‘put the question’ and the Tibetan line's ‘ask’. Should the note on 4a record his reading (perhaps pariccheda, ‘determination’)?

Song uha (2b, 5b): Munidatta twice has na ūhe, ‘I do not make out’, a first-person verb with an object (cp.29.m3, cp.29.m6), not the noun ‘reasoning’ as subject; the Tibetan line of 2b has dbyibs, ‘shape’. Is this worth revisiting in the draft lines, or only noting? I have proposed an entry, uha, which you may let go.

Song 2a baṭa and biṇāṇā: in Munidatta's paraphrase the novice yogin is the one who cannot discern (instrumental), not someone addressed, and what is hard to discern is ‘reality’, not consciousness (cp.29.m3). Does either bear on the draft's vocative ‘lad’ and its ‘consciousness’?

āgamaśāstre (cp.29.m4): the glossary lists it as a form of agama. Following the Tibetan (lung dang bstan bcos) I translate ‘scripture and treatises’ and mark only ‘scripture’. Should that form be dropped from the agama entry?

Song 1a: Munidatta (cp.29.m2) and the Tibetan line both take the couplet as ‘it is not being, nor nonbeing’ (that is, neither is reality), not ‘being does not come to be, nonbeing does not go’. I have flagged this only; does the draft's 1a need a note?
